title: What is Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) — restore a base backup then replay WAL/binlog up to a specific timestamp — and why is it critical for recovering from accidental deletes or corruption?

s1_definition.profdef: Point-in-Time Recovery restores a physical base backup and then replays the archived write-ahead log (or MySQL binlog) forward only up to a chosen target — a timestamp, transaction id, or named restore point. It lets you rewind the database to the exact moment just before a bad event, rather than only to the last full backup.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose at National Bank of India someone runs a wrong command at 2:05 PM that wipes Rajesh's transactions. A plain nightly backup only takes you back to midnight, losing a whole day. PITR is like a time machine: start from the midnight snapshot, then replay every recorded change up to 2:04 PM — one minute before the mistake — so you lose almost nothing.
s1_definition.oneliner: PITR = restore the base backup, then replay the log up to one instant before disaster.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Point-in-Time Recovery restores a physical base backup and then replays the archived write-ahead log (or MySQL binlog) forward only up to a chosen target — a timestamp, transaction id, or named restore point. It lets you rewind the database to the exact moment just before a bad event, rather than only to the last full backup.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose at National Bank of India someone runs a wrong command at 2:05 PM that wipes Rajesh's transactions. A plain nightly backup only takes you back to midnight, losing a whole day. PITR is like a time machine: start from the midnight snapshot, then replay every recorded change up to 2:04 PM — one minute before the mistake — so you lose almost nothing.

**One line to remember:** PITR = restore the base backup, then replay the log up to one instant before disaster.

sections.s2_technical:
PITR requires two ingredients kept continuously: a physical base backup and an unbroken archive of WAL/binlog segments from that base onward. To recover, you restore the base into a fresh data directory, then configure a recovery target — `recovery_target_time = '2026-10-25 14:04:00'` (or a transaction id, LSN, or named point) — and the engine replays WAL in order, stopping exactly at the target.

Why it is critical: full backups alone only restore to their capture time, so any work since then is lost, and logical mistakes like an accidental DELETE or a bad migration are not caught by replication (which faithfully copies the mistake). PITR targets the moment just before the bad transaction, recovering everything up to it. It also rescues from corruption by replaying to a clean point.

Senior nuance: the Recovery Point Objective is bounded by how frequently and reliably WAL is archived — gaps break the replay chain. Use named restore points before risky operations, keep base backups and WAL in durable off-site storage, and rehearse PITR so the Recovery Time Objective is known. For logical deletes you often PITR into a side instance, extract the lost rows, and merge them back rather than rewinding production wholesale.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A bad script at National Bank of India deletes Rajesh's transactions at 2:05 PM. The nightly backup is from midnight. This is exactly what PITR solves: restore midnight, replay WAL to 2:04 PM.

The demo has a `PitrEngine` that holds a base snapshot and an ordered WAL list, and `recoverTo(targetTime)` replays only entries up to the target, showing the deletion at 2:05 is skipped so Rajesh's rows survive.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__pitr_note.sql (PostgreSQL PITR setup, illustrative)
-- Enable continuous archiving on the primary:
--   wal_level = replica
--   archive_mode = on
--   archive_command = 'cp %p /wal_archive/%f'
-- Recover: restore base backup, then set recovery target:
--   restore_command = 'cp /wal_archive/%f %p'
--   recovery_target_time = '2026-10-25 14:04:00'
-- Named restore point before a risky migration:
SELECT pg_create_restore_point('before_ledger_migration');
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
pitr:
  base-backup: s3://nbi-db-backups/base/2026-10-25-0000
  wal-archive: s3://nbi-db-backups/wal/
  default-target: latest        # or a timestamp / restore point
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a midnight base snapshot, WAL inserting two transactions at 10:00 and 13:00, and a destructive DELETE at 14:05; recovery target is 14:04.

Step 1: Restore starts from the base snapshot containing only the opening entry.

Step 2: Replay applies the 10:00 and 13:00 inserts because they are before the target, rebuilding txn-A and txn-B.

Step 3: On reaching the 14:05 DELETE, which is after the target, replay stops, so the destructive operation is never applied and Rajesh's transactions survive.

```text
2026-10-25 18:36:00 [INFO] PITR restore base, replay WAL up to 2026-10-25T14:04
2026-10-25 18:36:00 [INFO] replayed 2026-10-25T10:00 INSERT txn-A SAV2001
2026-10-25 18:36:00 [INFO] replayed 2026-10-25T13:00 INSERT txn-B SAV2001
2026-10-25 18:36:00 [WARNING] STOP at 2026-10-25T14:05 (DELETE all txn) — beyond target, skipped
recovered state -> [SAV2001 opening, txn-A SAV2001, txn-B SAV2001]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  base backup (00:00)
    │ replay WAL in order
    ▼
  10:00 INSERT txn-A ✓
  13:00 INSERT txn-B ✓
  ─── recovery_target_time = 14:04 ───
  14:05 DELETE all txn  ✗ (after target → STOP)
    ▼
  recovered DB = state as of 14:04 (mistake avoided)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — PitrEngine ═══

  ┌─ Pattern: restore base + ordered log replay to a target instant ─┐
  │  SOLID S: engine only reconstructs state up to the target        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          PitrEngine          │
  │  - baseSnapshot: List        │  state at backup time
  │  - wal: List<WalEntry>       │  ordered changes
  │  + recoverTo(target): List   │  replay; STOP at target
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract recoverTo:
    Pre:  continuous WAL from base to target (no gaps)
    Post: state == DB at target; entries after target not applied
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Point-in-Time Recovery restores a physical base backup and then replays the archived write-ahead log, or the MySQL binlog, forward only up to a chosen target such as a timestamp, a transaction id, or a named restore point. That means I can rewind the database to the exact instant just before a bad event instead of only to the last full backup, which is why it is critical for accidental deletes, bad migrations, and corruption — mistakes that replication would otherwise faithfully copy.

In our National Bank of India platform I keep continuous WAL archiving alongside daily base backups, and when a bad script deleted a day of transactions at five past two, I restored the midnight base into a fresh instance and set the recovery target to one minute before the deletion, so replay rebuilt every real transaction and simply stopped before the destructive one. The things I watch are that the Recovery Point Objective is bounded by how reliably WAL is archived — any gap breaks the replay chain — so I store base backups and WAL off-site, create named restore points before risky operations, and rehearse recovery to know the Recovery Time Objective. For a targeted logical delete I often recover into a side instance, extract the lost rows, and merge them back rather than rewinding all of production. The line I remember is: restore the base backup, then replay the log up to one instant before disaster.
